meta.titre: Arithmetic: Factors, HCF, LCM, BODMAS and Standard Form
meta.sous_theme: Prime factors, HCF and LCM, BODMAS, standard form

sections.contenu_markdown: A wholesaler in Douala has 72 kg of rice and 180 kg of beans. He wants to pack both into identical sacks, each filled with one kind of food only, with no food left over. What is the largest possible sack? Elsewhere in the same town, two minibuses leave the park together and come back at different intervals: when will they be together again? These everyday questions are answered by the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple. They appear in GCE Paper 1 every year, together with place value, ordering numbers, BODMAS and standard form.

items: A prime number has exactly two factors, $1$ and itself: $2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, \dots$ (the number $1$ is not prime).
The multiplication tables up to $12\times 12$ are known by heart.
On a number line, a number further to the left is smaller, so $-7<-3$.

sections.titre: Prime factors, HCF, LCM, BODMAS and standard form
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Prime factorisation.** Write a number as a product of primes using a factor tree or repeated division. Always use index notation: $72=2^{3}\times 3^{2}$ and $180=2^{2}\times 3^{2}\times 5$.

**HCF (highest common factor).** The largest number that divides exactly into both numbers. Take the **common** primes, each with its **smallest** power.

**LCM (lowest common multiple).** The smallest number that both numbers divide into. Take **every** prime that appears, each with its **greatest** power.

For two numbers $a$ and $b$: $\ \text{HCF}\times\text{LCM}=a\times b$. This is a useful check.

**BODMAS.** Work in this order: Brackets, Orders (powers and roots), Division and Multiplication (left to right), Addition and Subtraction (left to right). So $8+2\times 5=18$, not $50$.

**Place value and ordering.** Compare negative numbers by their position on the number line: the more negative number is the smaller one.

**When to choose which.** Use the **HCF** when you *split into equal groups with nothing left over* (largest size of a group). Use the **LCM** when events *repeat and must meet again* (first time together).

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a very large or very small number must be written compactly.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
A number is in standard form when written as $a\times 10^{n}$ with $1\le a<10$ and $n$ a whole number.

- $45\,000=4.5\times 10^{4}$ (the point moves 4 places left, so $n=4$).
- $0.00072=7.2\times 10^{-4}$ (the point moves 4 places right, so $n=-4$).

To multiply, multiply the numbers and add the powers: $(3.6\times 10^{5})\times(2.5\times 10^{-2})=9\times 10^{3}$.

variantes.nom: Finding an unknown number from HCF and LCM
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the HCF, the LCM and one of the two numbers are given.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use $\text{HCF}\times\text{LCM}=a\times b$ and solve for the missing number. If the HCF is $4$, the LCM is $48$ and one number is $12$, the other is $\dfrac{4\times 48}{12}=16$.

sections.enonce_markdown: A trader packs $72$ kg of rice and $180$ kg of beans into sacks. Every sack holds the same mass and contains one kind of food only. (a) What is the greatest mass of one sack? Two minibuses leave the Mvan park together at 6:00 am. One returns to the park every $72$ minutes and the other every $180$ minutes. (b) At what time are they next at the park together?

etapes.action: Write both numbers as products of primes.
etapes.justification: Prime factors make the common and the extra factors easy to see.
Equal sacks with nothing left over means the sack mass must divide both $72$ and $180$; we want the greatest. Take the common primes with the smallest powers.
The buses meet again after a time that is a multiple of both $72$ and $180$; we want the first one. Take all primes with the greatest powers.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The greatest mass of a sack is $36$ kg, and the minibuses are next together at the park at 12:00 noon.

items.pourquoi_faux: $36$ is the LCM. The HCF is a factor of both numbers, so it can never be larger than either number.
On the number line $-7$ lies to the left of $-3$, so it is the smaller number.
Multiplication is done before addition (BODMAS). Working from left to right ignores this rule.
In standard form the first number must be at least $1$ and less than $10$.

items.erreur_markdown: $36=4\times 9$, so these are its prime factors.
items.pourquoi_faux: $4$ and $9$ are not prime. A prime factorisation uses primes only.

items.solution_markdown:
(a) Brackets first: $7-4=3$. Then the power: $3^{2}=9$. Then multiplication and division from the left: $3\times 9=27$, and $27\div 9=3$. Finally $20-3=17$.

**Answer: $17$.**

(b) Move the point $4$ places to the right to get $7.2$, so $0.00072=7.2\times 10^{-4}$.

**Answer: $7.2\times 10^{-4}$.**

items.enonce_markdown: Two street lamps at a junction in Bamenda flash together at midnight. One flashes every $60$ seconds and the other every $84$ seconds. (a) Find the HCF and LCM of $60$ and $84$. (b) After how many seconds do they next flash together? (c) How many times do they flash together during the next hour, not counting the flash at midnight?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $60=2^{2}\times 3\times 5$ and $84=2^{2}\times 3\times 7$.

$\text{HCF}=2^{2}\times 3=12$ and $\text{LCM}=2^{2}\times 3\times 5\times 7=420$. Check: $12\times 420=5040=60\times 84$.

(b) They flash together again after the LCM: **$420$ seconds** ($7$ minutes).

(c) One hour is $3600$ seconds and $3600\div 420\approx 8.57$. So they flash together at $420, 840, \dots, 8\times 420=3360$ seconds, and the next one ($3780$ s) is after the hour.

**Answer: $8$ times.**

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) The HCF of two numbers is $6$ and their LCM is $180$. One of the numbers is $36$. Find the other number.

(b) Without a calculator, evaluate $(3.6\times 10^{5})\times(2.5\times 10^{-2})$, giving your answer in standard form.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\text{HCF}\times\text{LCM}=\text{product of the two numbers}$, so $6\times 180=36\times N$.

$N=\dfrac{1080}{36}=30$. Check: $36=2^{2}\times 3^{2}$ and $30=2\times 3\times 5$ give $\text{HCF}=2\times 3=6$ and $\text{LCM}=2^{2}\times 3^{2}\times 5=180$.

**Answer: $30$.**

(b) $3.6\times 2.5=9$ and $10^{5}\times 10^{-2}=10^{3}$, so the product is $9\times 10^{3}$, which already has $1\le 9<10$.

**Answer: $9\times 10^{3}$.**

items_markdown: Write numbers as products of primes in index form: for example $72=2^{3}\times 3^{2}$.
**HCF**: common primes, smallest powers (equal groups, largest size). **LCM**: all primes, greatest powers (events meeting again).
BODMAS: brackets, powers, then $\times$ and $\div$, then $+$ and $-$, working left to right inside each level.
Standard form is $a\times 10^{n}$ with $1\le a<10$; negative powers are for small numbers.
